Coppersmith
KOP-er-smith
n. (a worker in copper or brass; the trade of Alexander, who withstood Paul)
From copper and smith. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Paul's last letter, naming both the man and his trade: Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil.

Biblical Definition

Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works: of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words. Paul is writing from a Roman prison near the end of his life, and the passage around this verse is the most personal in his letters. Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world. Only Luke is with me. Bring the cloke that I left at Troas, and the books, but especially the parchments. And then Alexander, named with his trade so Timothy will know exactly which man to avoid. Paul does not take the reckoning into his own hands: the Lord reward him according to his works is a committal, not a curse pronounced by Paul's authority, and it matches his own rule in Romans to give place unto wrath. What follows is the more remarkable half. At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge. He asks judgment for the opposer and forgiveness for the deserters, and then says the thing that steadied him: notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): one whose occupation is to manufacture copper utensils; in Scripture, the trade of Alexander, who greatly withstood Paul's words.

expand to see more

COPPERSMITH, n. One whose occupation is to manufacture copper utensils.

SMITH, n. Literally, the striker, the beater; hence, one who works in metals.

WITHSTAND, v.t. To oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force.

FORSAKE, v.t. To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon; to depart from.

RECOMPENSE, n. An equivalent returned for anything given, done or suffered.

Key Scripture

2Ti 4:14 — "Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works:"

2Ti 4:15 — "Of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words."

2Ti 4:16 — "At my first answer no man stood with me, but all men forsook me: I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge."

2Ti 4:17 — "Notwithstanding the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me; that by me the preaching might be fully known, and that all the Gentiles might hear: and I was delivered out of the mouth of the lion."

Modern Corruption

Naming an opposer by name is treated as unloving, so that churches are left unwarned; Paul names Alexander and his trade in an inspired letter and tells Timothy plainly to beware of him.

expand to see more

There is a widespread conviction that Christian charity forbids identifying a particular man as dangerous. The Pastorals do it repeatedly: Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul delivered unto Satan that they may learn not to blaspheme; Hymenaeus and Philetus, who said the resurrection is past already and overthrew the faith of some; Demas, who forsook him; and here Alexander the coppersmith, identified by trade so there could be no mistake. The purpose is protective. A warning that cannot name anyone protects no one, and the shepherd's duty includes the wolves.

What keeps this from becoming a licence for personal feuding is the way Paul does it. He states the injury factually, hands the recompense to God rather than pursuing it himself, gives Timothy a practical instruction, and in the very next sentence prays that the men who abandoned him at his trial would not be charged with it. The dictionary takes that as the pattern: name what must be named, for the protection of the flock; leave vengeance to the Lord; and forgive the weak, who are not the same as the hostile.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek chalkeus (G5471), a worker in copper or brass; anthistemi (G436), to withstand or oppose; apodidomi (G591), to render or repay.

expand to see more

Greek chalkeus (G5471) — a worker in copper or brass; the one occurrence, 2 Timothy 4:14.

Greek anthistemi (G436) — to set oneself against, to withstand; he hath greatly withstood our words.

Greek apodidomi (G591) — to give back, to recompense; the Lord reward him according to his works.

Greek enkataleipo (G1459) — to abandon, to forsake utterly; all men forsook me.

Greek endunamoo (G1743) — to strengthen, to empower; the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me.

Usage

"“Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil” — the single occurrence, a man named by trade."

"“I pray God that it may not be laid to their charge” — the deserters forgiven."

"“the Lord stood with me, and strengthened me” — what remained when men did not."
